title: Do Generate–Verify–Repair Guards Improve LLM NetOps Outputs? A Paired Emulator Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=200 natural-language NetOps intents) to measure whether a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—hosted-LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic validation + ≤1 deterministic repair—improves the rate of emulator-executable network configurations relative to ungated LLM generation. Tasks targeted small single- and multi-device changes (MTU/VLAN/admin sequences) and were applied to a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator with a deterministic validator. Baseline ungated generation produced 199/200 emulator-executable outputs; the GVR guarded pipeline produced 200/200. Paired contingency: n11=199, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.0, 0.015], which excludes the preregistered target effect (15 percentage points). The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis of a meaningful GVR improvement was not supported in this setup. We clarify design choices that affect interpretation (notably the shared-initial-generation protocol), precisely define the success endpoint, report that the guarded pipeline invoked the deterministic repair stage exactly once, and discuss implications, limitations, and reproducibility artifacts.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as translating operator intent into device configurations, generating repair actions, and accelerating routine changes. However, fluent but incorrect outputs (hallucinations, structural/semantic errors) create operational risk when applied to live networks. Prior work therefore recommends pairing LLMs with deterministic validators, grounding layers, or iterative repair loops to reduce these risks. We preregistered and executed a focused, autonomy-locked paired experiment to answer a concrete question: Does a bounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline materially increase the proportion of emulator-executable configurations produced from natural-language NetOps intents compared with ungated LLM generation? Our contribution is (1) a preregistered, paired evaluation (n=200) executed against a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator with an explicit deterministic validator; (2) an evidence-backed analysis showing a near-ceiling baseline and a negligible absolute GVR improvement in this setting; and (3) a precise accounting of design choices (shared-generation), endpoint definitions, and artifact locations to support reproducibility and correct interpretation.
sections.related_work: Recent literature documents active research on LLM-driven NetOps (intent-to-configuration translation, co-pilot assistants) alongside recurring failure modes such as hallucination and schema violations [Nguyen et al., 2024; OpsEval-style evaluations]. Mitigation proposals include retrieval-augmented generation, live schema grounding, grammar- and constraint-aware decoding, and verifier-augmented generate–validate–repair architectures; these reduce but do not eliminate incorrect outputs in adjacent domains (NL2SQL, clinical RAG) and in early NetOps prototypes. Formal network-verification tools and NetKAT-style formalisms provide deterministic checks for reachability and isolation and are natural validators for generated configurations, though scalability and dynamic control-plane fidelity remain practical concerns. Our study situates itself in this body of work by experimentally quantifying the incremental benefit of a bounded GVR guard under an autonomy-locked, preregistered paired design and by providing the full artifact bundle for verification.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered the study (primary estimand: paired success-rate difference guarded − baseline; confirmatory set n=200 paired intents; repair budget ≤1 deterministic repair iteration) and froze analysis and retry policies before observing outcomes. Tasks: 200 synthetic natural-language intents curated to span single- and small multi-device changes (ACLs, MTU/VLAN and admin-state sequences) generated by a deterministic task generator; representative task manifests and validator traces are archived. Arms: (A) baseline ungated LLM generation; (B) guarded GVR pipeline comprising a shared initial candidate (single LLM generation per intent, shared across arms), deterministic validation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and up to one deterministic repair iteration when the validator reports violations. Rationale for shared-initial-generation: the preregistered execution contract constrained model-call budget (maximum 400) and adopted shared initial candidates to create a paired, comparator-controlled assessment of repair efficacy for the same initial model output. This choice reduces variance due to independent re-sampling but means the guarded arm repairs the same initial candidate that the baseline used rather than competing with an independently re-sampled baseline output. We document provider-call accounting and stage counts in the execution manifest (see execution/execution_manifest.json). Success endpoint (operational definition): success = the deterministic validator's post-application report of validity, recorded as validation_after.valid = true in validator traces after applying the generated configuration to the Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator. The validator performed syntactic parsing of CLI statements, required-command presence checks against the task's intent constraints, and a simulated final_state reachability check within the emulator model; representative validator traces (including parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and final_state) are archived under execution/scoring/ (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json). Analysis: primary test = exact McNemar two-sided on paired binary outcomes (as preregistered); paired bootstrap percentile CIs computed with 10,000 resamples (seed 1729). All prompts, provider traces, responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were archived.
sections.results: Execution and outcomes: we completed 400 model-condition episodes (200 paired intents) with no provider/API failures and with full artifact capture. Provider-call accounting: 201 hosted-model calls were used under the maximum budget of 400. The guarded pipeline invoked the deterministic repair stage exactly once (provider-call stage_counts report a single repair invocation); full provider-call traces and the repair-stage trace are archived in the execution manifest and provider-call directories (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/provider_calls/ per the archived manifest). Contingency counts and tests: baseline (ungated) successes = 199/200; guarded successes = 200/200. Pairwise contingency table: n11 = 199, n10 = 1 (guarded-only success), n01 = 0 (baseline-only), n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0 (analysis recorded as exact_mcnemar_two_sided); paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.015] (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Secondary analyses: because baseline success was near ceiling, there were effectively no uncorrected failures to populate the planned failure-taxonomy analyses; repair-iteration yield curves show a single repair invocation sufficed to reach 200/200 in the confirmatory set. No episodes required retries outside the preregistered retry policy.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: in this preregistered, emulator-grounded setting and for the selected synthetic intent family, ungated gpt-5-mini generation already produced near-perfect emulator-executable configurations and the bounded GVR guard yielded a minute absolute improvement (0.5 percentage points). The paired 95% CI [0.0, 0.015] excludes the preregistered target improvement of 15 percentage points, so the confirmatory hypothesis of a substantial GVR benefit is not supported here. Practical implications: the marginal value of GVR guarding depends strongly on task difficulty, model capability, and emulator/validator fidelity. A shared-initial-generation design reduces model-call cost and isolates repair effectiveness on the same candidate, but it also reduces the operational realism where independent generation would reflect concurrent, unguarded deployments; consequently, the result should be interpreted as a conservative test of repair efficacy on identical initial outputs rather than a test of two independently running pipelines. The single observed repair invocation suggests either that the model performed well on the curated tasks or that the synthetic task distribution aligned with the model's learned patterns; in harder, out-of-distribution, multivendor, or adversarial workloads, GVR architectures and more aggressive repair budgets may yield larger gains. Threats to validity and reproducibility: the task set is synthetic and limited in scope; a single model and a Dockerized emulator were used; and the shared-generation protocol reduces variance but affects generalizability. All artifacts (prompts, responses, validator traces, provider-call logs, analysis CSVs) are archived in the execution bundle for verification (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/).
sections.conclusion: We executed an autonomy-locked, preregistered paired experiment to quantify whether a bounded generate–verify–repair guard increases emulator-executable success rates for LLM-generated NetOps configurations. On 200 curated intents and using gpt-5-mini with a deterministic validator and a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator, ungated generation achieved 199/200 successes and the guarded GVR pipeline achieved 200/200; the paired difference (0.005) was not statistically significant for the preregistered target (15 pp), and the 95% CI excludes that target. The result does not contradict prior evidence that GVR architectures reduce hallucinations in harder settings; rather, it highlights that guard value is context dependent. Future work should evaluate independent-generation comparisons, broader multivendor command dialects, adversarial intents, and richer operational axes such as verification latency, rollback efficacy, and human-in-the-loop costs.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock defined by the initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human involvement prior to the lock was limited to (i) selecting the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and (ii) approving the master prompt and autonomy boundary; no manual human editing of technical content, figures, captions, references, results, or manuscript text occurred after the lock. The autonomous pipeline performed literature search and verification, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, artifact capture, analysis, internal peer-review checks, and manuscript drafting. Models and tooling: generation used gpt-5-mini via provider recorded in model_configuration.json (provider: openai_responses); deterministic validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5; execution used a Dockerized Mininet+FRR emulator. Orchestration adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration froze the primary estimand, sample size (n=200 paired intents), model-call budget, repair budget (≤1 repair iteration), analysis plan (exact McNemar two-sided with preregistered paired estimand), and retry policy; these settings were not altered post-lock. Execution: the run completed 400 episodes (200 paired intents) using 201 model calls, with a single recorded repair-stage invocation; full provider-call traces, validator traces, response files, analysis artifacts, and the execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/). All deviations from preregistration are recorded in the execution manifest; none altered the primary estimand or sample size.
limitations: Synthetic, curated task set focused on small single- and multi-device changes; not comprehensive of production NetOps workloads (multivendor CLIs, hardware idiosyncrasies, dynamic control-plane timing).
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) evaluated; findings do not imply multi-model generality.

Emulator (Dockerized Mininet+FRR) and deterministic validator model control-plane behavior but do not fully capture production runtime dynamics such as BGP convergence timing or vendor-specific runtime effects.
Preregistered repair budget limited to a single deterministic repair iteration in the confirmatory protocol; different repair strategies or additional iterations might yield different outcomes.

Shared-initial-generation design (single initial candidate per intent shared across arms) reduced model-call cost and isolated repair effectiveness on identical candidates but reduces external generalizability compared with independent re-sampling per arm.
Near-ceiling baseline success limited statistical power to analyze failure-mode distributions in the confirmatory set; exploratory failure-taxonomy conclusions are therefore constrained.
Adversarial or out-of-distribution intents (e.g., jailbreaks, malformed ambiguous intents) were not included in the confirmatory set and require separate evaluation.
